title: Apple Says OpenAI Is Destroying Evidence in Trade Secrets Case
content:
(Bloomberg) -- Apple Inc. escalated its legal battle against OpenAI, claiming in a new court filing that OpenAI is actively destroying crucial evidence and that former iPhone engineer Chang Liu "not only downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic but also used it in his work" at the AI company.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The court brief was filed Monday in support of Apple's motion for expedited pretrial fact-finding in the lawsuit, which accuses the ChatGPT maker of stealing trade secrets. OpenAI has pushed to have the case dismissed.
Liu, who left Apple for OpenAI in January, is central to the case. He is one of more than 400 former Apple employees who went to work for the AI company, which is making a foray into the market for hardware devices.
According to the latest filing, OpenAI "only recently" provided a key piece of evidence: An Apple-issued MacBook that Liu had been using since departing the company. An initial forensic analysis has found that "Mr. Liu and others at OpenAI were well aware" of his continued unauthorized access to Apple's third-party cloud storage providers, the filing said.
The laptop also contains evidence that Liu "sent instructions for destroying evidence to an OpenAI colleague who confirmed she would comply," Apple's lawyers said. A key part of Apple's original complaint accused OpenAI of encouraging Apple employees to share information, components, drawings and other materials related to unreleased products while taking steps to cover its tracks.
A representative for OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
OpenAI has maintained that it adhered to industrywide recruiting standards when interviewing candidates from Apple and insists that Liu was simply trying to help a former colleague at Apple when accessing the cloud data. It published text message excerpts to help bolster that argument.
Apple alleged in Monday's filing that OpenAI is dragging its feet on producing evidence. "The MacBook represents the very limited information defendants provided so far (and only after weeks of delay), and shows Apple is not conducting 'fishing expeditions' but that its trade secrets are being used and evidence is being destroyed," Apple's lawyers wrote.

report.summary: Apple accuses OpenAI of destroying evidence in a trade secrets lawsuit over a former engineer's alleged theft of confidential circuit schematics.
report.background: The dispute centers on Chang Liu, a former Apple chip engineer who joined OpenAI in January. Apple claims Liu downloaded a confidential circuit schematic before leaving and later used it in OpenAI hardware development work. Liu is one of more than 400 former Apple employees now at OpenAI, which is expanding into AI-powered devices. Apple's original lawsuit alleged OpenAI encouraged employees to share unreleased product information while covering its tracks. OpenAI has denied the allegations, argued it follows standard recruiting practices, and pushed for dismissal. Apple's new court filing escalates the case by alleging evidence destruction, citing a recently produced Apple-issued MacBook that reportedly shows Liu accessing Apple's cloud storage after departure and instructing an OpenAI colleague to destroy evidence. The case highlights growing tension as Apple and OpenAI compete in AI hardware and talent acquisition.
key_points: Apple filed a court brief Monday alleging OpenAI is destroying evidence and requested expedited pretrial fact-finding. Apple argues the newly produced MacBook demonstrates its lawsuit is based on real trade secret misuse, not a speculative fishing expedition.

Central to the case is former Apple engineer Chang Liu, who allegedly downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic and used it in his work at OpenAI. Apple says this shows direct misappropriation of trade secrets rather than accidental exposure.

OpenAI only recently provided the Apple-issued MacBook Liu used after leaving Apple. A forensic analysis reportedly revealed Liu and others at OpenAI were aware of his continued unauthorized access to Apple's third-party cloud storage providers.

The laptop allegedly contains messages where Liu sent instructions for destroying evidence to an OpenAI colleague, who confirmed she would comply. This is a serious escalation in Apple's claim that OpenAI took steps to cover its tracks.

OpenAI disputes the allegations, saying it followed industry-standard recruiting practices and that Liu was trying to help a former colleague when accessing Apple cloud data. OpenAI has published text message excerpts to support its side and is seeking dismissal of the case.
report.impact: This case could reshape how AI companies hire engineers from hardware rivals like Apple, especially as OpenAI ventures into physical devices. Developers should be cautious about retaining former-employer data or accessing corporate cloud accounts after departure, as forensic scrutiny is increasingly common. For the broader AI industry, the outcome may set precedents for trade secret enforcement and evidence preservation in talent-driven competition. Regular users may see slower or more cautious AI hardware development while legal battles unfold, and heightened tension between major players like Apple and OpenAI could influence future product collaborations or market strategies.
report.tools: For those following digital forensics and e-discovery in trade secret cases, tools like Magnet AXIOM, Cellebrite, and Guidance Software EnCase are commonly used for laptop and cloud data analysis. Open-source options include The Sleuth Kit (TSK) and Autopsy for disk imaging and forensic review. On the legal-tech side, Relativity and Everlaw help manage discovery documents, while cloud access logging from AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure can reveal unauthorized storage access patterns.
